https://www.thetimes.com/comment/columni.title: Why I’m demonstrating against Trump’s visit
https://www.thetimes.com/comment/columni.text:
The roll call of groups supporting Wednesday’s “Trump Not Welcome” demonstration in London is predictable and cringe-making, headed by Extinction Rebellion, CND, Greenpeace and Southall Black Sisters. It is the sort of gathering mocked as Rent-A-Mob.
Yet my wife and I plan to turn out with them because it seems right to stand up and get counted among the naysayers when the most deplorable of all US presidents arrives on his second state visit to Britain.
If I was Sir Keir Starmer, imperatives of state might induce me, too, to hang out the bunting. Such is Donald Trump’s appetite for fawning and flattery that this week’s shenanigans may dissuade him, for a while, from increasing trade tariffs on UK goods beyond his baseline 10 per cent. He could pause the barrage of insults he and his Maga friends heap on Europe, Britain included.
• Trump UK visit live: King Charles to host president at Windsor Castle
Not being Keir Starmer, however, the rest of us have no responsibility to pretend that we like it. This will be a visit inspired not by affection or respect on the part of the hosts but by fear — apprehension about what this president is capable of doing, what pain the most powerful man on earth might impose on us if we cause him grief or even irritation. To such a depth of weakness Britain has come that it is kowtowing with a Household Cavalry escort before a man whose conduct in office has brought shame on the United States.
Trump is inflicting death by a thousand cuts on Ukraine, progressively withdrawing support while refusing to break off his one-sided love affair with Vladimir Putin, even in the face of such outrageous provocations as last week’s Russian drone attack on Poland.
Trump, and Trump alone, arms Binyamin Netanyahu to sustain Israel’s persecution of the Palestinians. He has destroyed the trust in American good faith, judgment and reliability which has been the cornerstone of the western alliance since 1945.
His global vendettas include the imposition of 50 per cent tariffs on Brazil’s goods in an attempt to force its government to free his friend Jair Bolsonaro, the former president now convicted of attempting a coup against his 2022 election defeat. He continues to threaten Denmark with the seizure of Greenland. He has withdrawn the US from international bodies, cancelled funding for climate change measures and eviscerated US foreign aid and soft power.
But it is Trump’s assaults upon American democratic institutions which should cause every respecter of freedom most alarm. The deployment of the National Guard in the Democratic city strongholds of Washington and Los Angeles has nothing to do with crime prevention and everything to do with a symbolic flaunting of executive power.
Trump sacks from government bodies traditionally non-partisan appointees and replaces them with placemen and women, almost uniformly inadequate. He falsifies government data and cancels bodies charged with its impartial collation.
He employs as health secretary Robert Kennedy Jr, an enemy of science and of evidence as most educated people understand these things, who is bulldozing America’s defences against disease. Trump is also waging war on educational institutions which he regards as hostile to his purposes.
The most egregious and pernicious of his campaigns is against the legal system and, thus, against the US constitution’s checks and balances. Empowered by a supine Republican-dominated Congress and a Republican-packed Supreme Court, he ignores repeated findings against himself by federal judges, confident that his excesses will be rubber-stamped by the highest appellate body.
Judges customarily set out their findings over many pages, reinforced by precedents. Few of the Supreme Court’s recent decisions extend beyond paragraphs. The sorry creatures who occupy the seats once held by some of the greatest legal figures in US history eschew argument. They merely baldly assert that the president’s actions fall within the authority of the chief executive.
The FBI is exploited as Trump’s enforcement arm against personal enemies — the search of the house of John Bolton, his former aide and now foe, was only a conspicuous example. Canadians arriving at the US border are routinely subjected to harassment. A distinguished academic who lectured in Washington last month felt obliged to take an old iPhone: US immigration often seizes and examines personal databases, seeking evidence of criticism of the president to justify their owners’ exclusion.
Nobody should pretend any of this falls within the parameters of the normal. The actions catalogued above represent an attack on precedent, freedom and ultimately US democracy; on the nation’s historic role as an exemplar and standard bearer for values we all hold dear.
A few Europeans declare enthusiasm for Donald Trump. The rich love him because he is their man; he is making them richer still. He himself will be the first US president who, along with his family, will leave office incomparably wealthier than he entered it.
There are also those who say: “Whatever you think of Trump, he is doing a great job on expelling illegal immigrants.” Some of us respond: stop a minute. Think of the people who used such words in the past to justify acquiescing before arbitrary rulers who trampled upon human rights, decency, justice and freedom. And of what came of such indulgence.
The last time I participated in a demonstration was on October 27, 1968 when 100,000 people marched against the Vietnam War. I remember a policeman kicked me. This week the Hastingses will swallow our misgivings and demonstrate against this American’s supremely embarrassing presence in Britain.

https://www.thetimes.com/comment/columni.title: Climate cultists to blame for rising scepticism
https://www.thetimes.com/comment/columni.text:
There were no 40 degree days this summer. When I realised we’d got to September without hitting those sickly heights I was relieved — which is strange because until 2022 no such thing had ever happened in the UK. There was the brutal, record-breaking July (there were about 3,000 deaths associated with heatwaves that year), and suddenly 40 degrees was part of the new normal.
The hottest day this year was a mere 35.8 degrees. This summer was still, though, the warmest on record. It followed the warmest spring on record and, up to May, the driest spring for 100 years. That laid the conditions for wildfires on the Yorkshire Moors, while Britain’s farmers are predicted to have their fifth-worst harvest ever. The only consolation is that last year’s was even more appalling. Our seas broke heat records too.
It’s not a question any more of whether climate change is happening. It is, and you don’t have to be a farmer or a fisherman or even the kind of pasty Anglo-Saxon who melts into a helpless puddle as soon as the mercury hits 30C (hello!) to notice. It’s blazed across the landscape, which turned prematurely golden this year thanks to a “false autumn” caused by the stress on trees.
• Nature Notebook — Plant a tree: you never know where it might lead
But while all this is happening the public mood on climate change has started to shift, perversely, towards scepticism. According to polling for The Times, 25 per cent of Britons now believe the threat of a warming planet has been exaggerated, up from 16 per cent four years ago; 61 per cent believe it has not been exaggerated, down from 68 per cent.
The climate consensus hasn’t collapsed but it is crumbling. In the 2000s climate scientists bemoaned the media’s tendency to set everything up as a “debate”, meaning sceptics were given prominence that exceeded their credibility. From the vantage point of 2025 that sounds like a nice problem to have. Today the world’s biggest podcaster (Joe Rogan) is pushing outright untruths about “global cooling” to his millions of followers.
But blaming Rogan is futile: appealing counterfactual narratives are the lifeblood of podcasters and you may as well be angry with a weather system as be angry with Rogan. Similarly, it’s depressing to see Reform rush towards the rhetoric of “drill, baby, drill” (and the Conservatives tag along behind them), but did anyone seriously imagine Nigel Farage as an anti-carbon warrior?
The failure of environmentalism’s popularity is down to environmentalists — or at least to the radical wing of the movement. This is not for lack of energy. Since 2018 there has been an extraordinary outburst of activism around climate change. In 2019, Greta Thunberg, then 16, gave her tearful speech to the United Nations in which she accused the assembled adults of “stealing their children’s future in front of their very eyes”.
Thunberg inspired mass “school strikes” as adolescents demanded adults do more to confront the crisis. A year before, Extinction Rebellion had been established and began mobilising supporters into large-scale acts of civil disobedience in an attempt to “compel those in power to act”. In 2019, the group occupied Marble Arch, Parliament Square, Oxford Circus and Waterloo Bridge with the aim of seizing up traffic around London.
Just Stop Oil (founded, like Extinction Rebellion, by the longstanding activist Roger Hallam) has been even more attention-grabbing: in 2022 the group halted traffic on the M25 and two of its activists threw tomato soup over Van Gogh’s Sunflowers. But none of this matches the commitment of Sacrifice for Survival, whose members ran a short-lived campaign of setting themselves on fire in protest against UK domestic flights.
From the inside, all these acts must feel profoundly righteous — and justified by the severity of the situation. From the outside, they are at best infuriating and at worst deeply disturbing acts of self-harm. The environmental movement has become something closer to a cult, with its cast of child saints (Thunberg) and martyrs. Hallam even styles himself as “prophet” and has the unsettling bearing to match.
Cults like converts but even more than that they like outsiders: the impure ones against whom they can measure their own goodness. The tests one must pass to become one of the saved are ever-growing. It’s not enough to believe in human-caused climate change and want to take action to stop it. When you sign up to Extinction Rebellion you also sign up to a suite of leftist beliefs on trans rights and Gaza.
It suits Reform UK very nicely to position itself as the voice of growth and common sense, in contrast to Ed Miliband’s uninspiring climate technocratism and the “thousands of green jobs” that have so far failed to materialise. But given that the populist right wanted a culture war, why would the environmental movement choose to deliver one on a plate?
The answer has to be that the environmental radicals never wanted to win. As far as they’re concerned the apocalypse is already here: that’s why they use slogans like “five years to save the world”. The only thing left to do is make clear that they are on the side of good. The fire might be coming for everyone but at least they can feel superior as they burn.
The acts of Extinction Rebellion et al aren’t a sign of urgency: they’re a mark of despair. And nothing is more politically repellant than despair. Climate change is here but it’s still possible to mitigate its effects. The environmental movement has work to do. Time for it to stop behaving like a religious sect and start winning back hearts and minds.

https://www.thetimes.com/uk/politics/art.title: President Trump’s state visit with King Charles — as it happened
https://www.thetimes.com/uk/politics/art.text:
Sir Keir Starmer’s present to Trump was a symbol of British ministerial power in a colour the president has made his own.
Starmer gifted him a ministerial red box with the presidential seal and title embossed on it, according to ITV’s Robert Peston.
On Thursday morning, the president and first lady will formally bid farewell to the King and Queen at Windsor Castle before splitting up for the morning.
Trump will meet Starmer and his wife at Chequers, the prime minister’s 16th-century manor house where he will be greeted by bagpipers and a Guard of Honour from RAF Halton.
He and Starmer will view the Sir Winston Churchill archives held at the residence, before holding a bilateral meeting. The pair will then join a business reception hosted by Rachel Reeves, the chancellor, before a joint press conference at Chequers.
The Queen and Melania will view Queen Mary’s dolls’ house — the largest in the world, complete with running water and electricity — and visit the royal library.
Melania will then join the Princess of Wales at Frogmore Gardens to meet the chief scout, Dwayne Fields.
The first lady will rejoin Trump at Chequers and Lord Chamberlain, the most senior officer of the royal household, will bid them farewell on behalf of the King.
When President Trump and his wife, Melania, landed in the UK on Tuesday night, the first lady wore a floor-sweeping Burberry trench coat. If you don’t have a driver, don’t even think about it.
It was thoughtfully selected, given that the label has launched a collection inspired by the King’s Highgrove gardens: a perfect state banquet talking point. Yet this was not the sensible knee or calf-length variety you or I might buy if we had £2,490 ($3,400) to spare.
The first lady’s is believed to be from a 2020 collection created by Riccardo Tisci, the label’s designer at the time, and comes in an ultra-elite 1 per cent cut: so deliberately long as to require a driver and the innate confidence of the chauffeured that they will avoid puddles. A lady’s maid might be useful too, although, helpfully, Mrs Trump III stands at a catwalk-friendly 5ft 11in, so the only drag being spoken of during this visit will be the fiscal variety.
Read in full: Meet the limo hem — Melania Trump’s mac is only for the 1%

President Trump praised the “extraordinary graciousness” of the royal family in their welcome. “I hope it is the last time,” a president is invited twice to the UK on a state visit, he joked.
He applauded the King’s ability to remember the names of “every single person” in the room, and said: “Some of them had bad names like ‘XYZ-Q3’ and he knew every one of them, or at least I think he did, because nobody was complaining. I was very impressed with that.”
Addressing the King directly, Trump said: “This is truly one of the highest honours of my life, I have such respect for you and such respect for your country for many decades.”
“Together we have done more for humanity than any two countries”, he added. He thanked the King and Queen and sat down as the British national anthem played.
The King has praised the “enduring bond” between the US and the UK in a speech to guests at the royal banquet.
“It is remarkable to think how far we have come,” he went on. “My five times great-grandfather did not spare his words when he spoke of the revolutionary leaders.” Trump laughed at the mention of the Wars of Independence.
“I have cherished the close ties between the British and America people”, he said.
Charles joked that he might have been married off to Tricia Nixon, the daughter of former president Richard Nixon, if the American media had had its way 50 years ago.
“Together we laid the foundations of nuclear science and built the internet”, he added. “Together our scientists are shaping the world of tomorrow,” he said, in an apparent nod to the many tech industry bosses in attendance.
He then moved onto one of his favourite subjects, the importance of conserving nature, before toasting as the US national anthem played.
King Charles, Queen Camilla, President Trump and the first lady will be joined by a glittering selection of Britons and Americans across politics, business and sport, as well as members of the royal family.
A Royal Procession of special guests will join nearly 120 other invitees in Windsor Castle’s St George’s Hall, which staff have been preparing for three days.
The Prince and Princess of Wales, Princess Anne, Vice Admiral Sir Tim Laurence and the Duke and Duchess of Gloucester will be seated alongside members of Trump’s inner circle and business bosses, with interests on both sides of the pond. Sir Keir Starmer and his wife, Victoria, will also attend.
Also in attendance will be the newspaper tycoon Rupert Murdoch; Dame Vivian Hunt, the British-American business executive; Lori Huang, the wife of the Nividia boss Jensen Huang; Tim Cook, the chief executive of Apple; Charles Woodburn, chief executive of BAE Systems; Jane Fraser, chief executive of Citigroup bank; Sir Richard Moore, head of MI6; Dame Katherine Grainger, Olympian and the chancellor of Glasgow University.
Melania Trump chose an eye-catching yellow gown with a light pink belt for the imminent state banquet.
She was photographed alongside her husband, dressed in traditional white tie, and the King and Queen, who both wore navy blue sashes and official medals.
The Prince and Princess of Wales have arrived for the banquet, in white tie formal occasion wear to mark Trump’s visit.
Kate chose a sweeping white and gold lace gown, with a red and blue sash and a diamond tiara, while William was dressed in a white bow tie with red cuffs and a blue sash.
The pair also wore their official badges and medals for the event.

Trump has often said he is a deeply musical person and took up the flute as a child, a former hobby he shares with the British prime minister.
The music for the banquet features a predictable blend of British orchestral and folk favourites, American standards, musical anthems and James Bond soundtracks.
The Rolling Stones’ You Can’t Always Get What You Want will rub shoulders with Liberty Bell and music from West Side Story.
Elton John, whose music Trump loves, is represented on the set list with Tiny Dancer, while traditional Irish and Scottish music may remind the president of his ancestral ties to Britain.
Royal chefs have been busy conjuring personal touches for the menu to delight the King’s guests.
After dinner, guests will be served Warre’s 1945 Vintage Port, in recognition of Trump as the 45th, as well as the 47th, president of the United States.
The attendees will also enjoy Hennessy 1912 Cognac Grande Champagne, from the President’s Scottish mother’s birth year, and Bowmore Queen’s Cask 1980, Islay, a gift to the late Queen Elizabeth in 1980, which was bottled for her Golden Jubilee in 2002.
A cocktail has also been designed for the occasion, called the Transatlantic Whisky Sour, a twist on the classic Whisky Sour.
The Palace says it blends the smoky depth of Johnnie Walker Black with the bright citrus of marmalade. Crowned with a pecan foam and garnished with a toasted marshmallow set on a star-shaped biscuit, it evokes “the warmth of a fireside S’more”.
The menu enjoyed by the royals and their guests at the banquet tonight has been built using produce from three English counties.
For starters, the royal family, politicians and business heads will be served a Hampshire watercress panna cotta with parmesan shortbread and quail ggg salad.
Next, the guests will enjoy organic Norfolk chicken ballotine wrapped in courgettes, with a thyme and savoury infused jus. This will be followed by a vanilla ice cream bombe with a Kentish raspberry sorbet interior and lightly poached Victoria plums.
To accompany the meal, guests will drink a selection of English, Californian, and French wines. Trump, who has never drunk alcohol, will presumably be given a choice of soft drinks. He is known to be a fan of Diet Coke.
The White House shared a photograph of President Trump with King Charles from Windsor Castle.
The pair enjoyed a day of military fanfare, pomp and procession complete with a visit to Queen Elizabeth II’s tomb. Tonight they will sit down for an elaborate state banquet.
Demonstrations in central London are drawing to a close, after police moved to disperse the remaining protesters from Parliament Square, where up to 5,000 reportedly gathered.
Extinction Rebellion campaigners played drums and people chanted “Free Palestine” as they slowly walked away.
A very small counter protest — formed of eight people — waved Israeli, American, Iranian and Union Jack flags. They were held apart from the Stop Trump protestors by barriers and police and heckled with the other side over Palestine and the death of Charlie Kirk.
Zoe Gardiner, of the Stop Trump Coalition, said: “This is our country and we don’t want Trump, we don’t want Farage, we don’t want the far right”, before leading a chant of “migrants welcome, Trump f*** off”.
The armed forces will identify targets on the battlefield in any future war using technology created by Palantir, a data-mining company linked to the CIA, under a £750 million deal to be signed during President Trump’s state visit, The Times can disclose.
British commanders will be able to efficiently eliminate enemy forces using a highly sensitive system powered by artificial intelligence, part of moves designed to change the way the military fights.
The deal, which is said to include a commitment by the US company to invest £1.5 billion in the UK over five years, has been rushed through to coincide with Trump’s visit, sources said.
Read in full: Trump visit brings £750m Palantir deal for military AI technology
The historian and Times columnist Sir Max Hastings, who was out protesting in London this afternoon, said Wednesday was a “humiliating day for Britain”.
He told Times Radio: “I’ve been with the protesters for the last two hours and I’ve shaken the hands of an awful lot of Times readers who feel the same way as I do. I think the only big disappointment about the demonstration has been that it’s been too diffuse, really, in some ways to be effective.
“We’ve got anti-racism, Ukraine, everybody else mixed up with all this, and especially an awful lot of pro-Palestinian demonstrators and whatever our sympathies may be with the cause I think the demo would have been more effective if it had been solely and exclusively about Donald Trump.
“But I’ve been very moved this afternoon by how many people have said to me that they feel as deeply and passionately as I do that it’s a humiliating day for Britain, that we have to entertain this dreadful man.”
Joseph Afafrane, 61, a security officer from Battersea, started his day in Windsor at 6am in a suit covered in union jacks and US flags.
“I love Trump and I love the royal family, that’s why I’m here to show support,” he said. “I saw him during his first visit visit in 2019, at Buckingham Palace. I was moving the flag and he waved me right back again. Trust me, he’s very nice.”
“I like a president, or a leader, who loves his people, who listens to his people, who listens to the working class people.”
The King and Queen will host a state dinner in St George’s Hall at Windsor Castle this evening. They have both personally checked the banquet table ahead of the dinner, scheduled for about 8pm.
In video shared on the Royal Family’s official X account, the King and Queen surveyed a vast table adorned with gold candles, huge floral centrepieces and polished crockery.
Pink, purple and yellow blooms covered the 50m table. The monarchs shook hands with the staff in appreciation for their hard work.
Charles and Trump are due to give speeches at the banquet which will also feature fanfares by The State Trumpeters of The Household Cavalry, as well as performances by The Duchess of Edinburgh’s String Orchestra, comprising musicians from the Royal Corps of Army Music.
Two people have been arrested near Windsor today over incidents thought to be linked to the president’s visit.
A woman was arrested for assaulting an emergency worker and using abusive language, while a man was arrested on suspicion of assault.
There was a heavy police presence outside the grounds for the president’s visit as well as a small gathering of both Trump fans and protesters.
The former Labour leader Jeremy Corbyn addressed the Stop Trump Coalition rally in London today.
He congratulated those who projected images of Donald Trump and the late paedophile Jeffrey Epstein onto Windsor Castle, for which four people have reportedly been arrested.
“There’s something very sinister about our times when people are prevented from expressing their views,” he said. “They take our right to protest because they don’t want us to protest.”
The royal family have marked President Trump’s wreath tribute at Queen Elizabeth’s tomb with a brief statement.
Writing via their official X account, they said: “This afternoon, The President and Mrs. Trump laid a wreath at the Tomb of Queen Elizabeth II. The President and the First Lady spent time with The late Queen during their State Visit in 2019.
“Following Her Majesty’s death in 2022, President Trump released a tribute to her, saying: ‘Melania and I will always cherish our time together with the Queen, and never forget Her Majesty’s generous friendship, great wisdom, and wonderful sense of humor. What a grand and beautiful lady she was—there was nobody like her!’”
Zarah Sultana, the MP for Coventry South, criticised the royal reception for Trump and used today’s rally in London to condemn the Unite the Kingdom march on the weekend, attended by more than 100,000 people.
She said protesters, organised by the far-right activist Tommy Robinson, “marched with the backing of international figures of the far-right”, and included Trump among them.
Sultana also took the opportunity to call “shame” on Washington for “enabling the genocide” in Gaza.
Britain rolling out the red carpet for Israeli politicians and now Trump, she said, is morally indefensible: “We say not in our name to Keir Starmer grovelling to US empire … These are our streets, our country, our future.”
Spontaneous chants of “Donald Trump has got to go”, and “When our rights are under attack, what do we do? Stand up, fight back”, broke out amongst the crowd of protesters as they marched towards the Parliament Square to reconvene.
The musician Billy Bragg performed songs aimed at Trump featuring the lyrics “you fascists are bound to lose”. The president came to Britain because he “wants to feel like a king”, Bragg claimed.
Nish Kumar, the comedian, launched a blow up ball with the vice president JD Vance’s face on it into the crowd. “Donald Trump is a lightning rod [for] white supremacist groups and racists around the world,” he said.
President Trump is “political Marmite”, the Conservative MP for Windsor has said.
Jack Rankin MP insisted that although the president might be divisive, he is very welcome in his constituency for the state visit at Windsor Castle.
“Donald Trump is political Marmite, and it might not be the case that if Windsor were a US state it would award him our electoral college votes — but that isn’t the point,” he said.
“He is here as the president of the United States, an institution we respect, and at the invitation of his majesty the King as his guest: as such, he is very welcome in Windsor.”
A flypast of the Red Arrows shot past Windsor Castle with a trail of red, white and blue smoke as Land of Hope and Glory came to an end.
The audience, including the prime minister and the King, applauded as the ceremony was brought to a close with Auld Lang Syne.
The crowd outside the castle cheered and whooped as the Red Arrows flew overhead. A handful of Trump fans wearing Maga hats chanted: “USA USA USA!”
A local family who had come to see the flypast said they “loved it”, although it was a bit “short and sweet”. Their toddler said: “It looked like a rainbow.”
Sir Keir Starmer and his wife Lady Starmer arrived at Windsor Castle for the Beating Retreat ceremony.
It takes place annually at the Horse Guards Parade in June, but this is the first time the parade has been performed during a state visit.
The Massed Bands of the Royal Marines, the Coldstream Guards and the Royal Air Force with the Old Guard Fifes and Drums from the US Army Band are on parade.
The songs have been chosen to reflect Trump’s Scottish roots, as well as British and American history.
When Trump first met the late Queen in 2018, he is said to have told his wife he felt he had made it in life. On his historic second state visit, the president has laid a wreath at her tomb inside St George’s Chapel.
The pair were given a tour of the historic building, including Henry VIII’s burial vault and a memorial plate in honour of Sir Winston Churchill. The president said: “This was a great honour.”
A herd of deer crossed the path of Dan Scavino, a White House deputy chief of staff, this morning as the president’s motorcade made its way up the Long Walk.
Dozens of the animals, which roam free in the vast Windsor Great Park, streamed across the road metres from the leading police motorcycle.
A flypast of F-35 jets above Windsor Castle has been cancelled due to poor weather. It was due to mark the first time British and US aircraft had jointly taken part in a state visit. A show of the Red Arrows will still go ahead.
Steve Lachooa, 34, from Woking, wore a Maga hat while waiting for the aircraft outside Windsor Castle. “I’m here in support of Donald Trump,” he said. “This guy’s actually making a change, whereas other presidents or prime ministers, they don’t care.”
“I want everything to change here in the UK, but it’s not going to because Starmer’s stubborn,” he said. “I hope he resigns or gets unelected somehow and Farage gets in.”
Speeches at the Stop Trump Coalition march were opened by Seema Syeda, a spokeswoman, who led chants including: “Donald, Donald you can’t hide / We charge you with genocide”, “Say it loud, say it clear / Donald Trump’s not welcome here” and “From the river to the sea / Palestine will be free.”
She criticised the “lavish dinner” prepared for Trump at Windsor Castle, while “people in Gaza starve”.
She was joined by speakers from groups such as Green New Deal Rising, Abortion Rights, the Ukraine Solidarity Campaign, the Make Them Pay Coalition, Democrats Abroad and a Cuban solidarity group.
The president and first lady joined the King and Queen to inspect artefacts pertaining to British-American relations.
“Wow,” Trump said as he looked at documents about US independence. “That’s fascinating,” said Charles as he pointed out another table, detailing the transatlantic cable used for communication between the two countries. Trump agreed: “That’s so amazing.”
The president and first lady were also shown a handwritten letter to the future Queen Elizabeth II from her mother, describing a picnic at President Franklin Roosevelt’s home in 1939.
An even older message, written by Queen Victoria to President James Buchanan in 1858, was included — describing the “common interest and esteem” between Britain and the US. The tickertape note was relayed using an undersea cable stretching from Ireland to Newfoundland, a landmark joint venture between the two countries.
The monarch normally gets to choose from four menus for a state banquet, which takes months of preparation, according to a former royal chef to Queen Elizabeth II.
As Trump, the royal family and 160 other guests prepare to sit down for the state banquet at Windsor Castle tonight, Darren McGrady said the chefs would plan for all contingencies.
“We’d always prepare extra food just in case anything did happen, like one of the footmen dropped a tray or some of the guests got overexcited and took three or four portions onto a plate. So we always had to allow for extra portions, timing and everything else,” he told Times Radio.
After lunch, the royal family will show the president and first lady a special display of the Royal Collection items relating to the United States and the UK.
The items were laid out in the Green Drawing Room, the semi-state room which is often used as the backdrop for official royal photographs.
It is where the wedding photographs of the Duke and Duchess of Sussex were taken in 2018. The Queen and Duke of Edinburgh were also pictured there to commemorate the Diamond Jubilee.
Designed for King George IV, the Green Drawing Room was originally known as the Library.
It features striking silk green wall hangings, which match the fabric of the antique settees and chairs, and elaborate gilded panels and doors. The Green Drawing Room was one of the rooms damaged in the 1992 Windsor Castle fire, but its carpet, which was shown at the Great Exhibition in 1851, survived the blaze
At the London protests, Blam, an artist, has made signs depicting Trump wearing Speedos with various tattoos referencing his relationship with President Putin, Jeffrey Epstein and criminal cases against him.
Auriel Dowry Granville, here with the climate group Merton Friends of the Earth, was dressed as “the Statue of Taking Liberties”.
“Donald Trump is a climate change denier and the biggest threat to humanity is climate change,” the 82-year-old said. “Trump is the most powerful man on the planet, if he would please listen to scientists he could really help path a way forward, instead of saying ‘drill baby drill’.”
When Sir Keir Starmer handed President Trump a letter from the King in February, the American leader paused.
Then, accepting the invitation to Britain contained therein, he said it would be a “great, great honour” and that staying at Windsor would be “really something”.
Where Barack Obama and George W Bush were invited for tea or lunch, for Trump the royals have rolled out the red carpet again.
• Read in full: All the key timings and events
Helen Scalway, 78, “cut up a good pillow case” to make her sign for a protest against President Trump’s visit, which read: “Trump, paedophile, crook. Not wanted here.”
She added: “I am completely shocked he was welcomed by Starmer. I think it is an absolute disgrace. I know he must be concerned about jobs but other European countries are finding other markets. We have sold our souls for the jobs that are involved there. Trump is a liar and he’s not welcome here.”
This is the first protest that Martin Edwardes, 72, has been to that isn’t a Pride march. He said: “His policies on Gaza are reprehensible and his policy on Ukraine is improbable and then there’s what he’s done to the poor people in America. I don’t think [the protest] will change Britain’s direction but hopefully it’s enough to let Trump know he’s not liked here. I hope it annoys him.”
Holding a sign which reads “Grannies against Trump”, Susie Park, 71, joked that she thought that this message would “strike fear into Trump’s heart”.
Sir Alan Duncan, the former international development minister who was involved in Trump’s first state visit in 2019, said the US president “will be happier than a youngster in Disney World”.
As Trump started his historic second state visit to the UK, Duncan said the US president’s love of the pomp and ceremony of the royal family should be used to the UK’s advantage.
“It’s good that we’re doing it. It’s fantastic that he likes the royal family so much, and so he should,” he told Times Radio. “I think Trump will be happier than a youngster in Disney World, frankly. It was beautifully done, could not have been done better, and very dignified.”
Duncan said while there were some critics of the US president receiving a second state visit, it was important to make sure we have a “good relationship with the most important country in the world”
An American dressed as the “QAnon Shaman”, bearing US and Israel flags, shouted at an artist who had painted Trump as a caveman. “I don’t like that,” he said, “You’re mocking him. How dare you mock the greatest president, Donald Trump?”
When Kaya Mar, the political satire artist, said the president was narcissistic, the American made fun of his pronunciation.
The American, who gave his name as Shaman Shimshan, said he was from Texas but lived in the UK. “I’m here to welcome the president Donald Trump,” he said, “This is going to be a grand alliance between England and the US.”
The King and Queen have presented President Trump with a bespoke handbound, specially crafted book to celebrate the 250th anniversary of the US declaration of independence, which will be marked next year.
Their majesties have also gifted their US guests with the union flag which flew above Buckingham Palace on the day of Trump’s second inauguration on January 20, 2025.
To the first lady, the King and Queen gifted a personalised Anya Hindmarch handbag and a silver and enamel bowl from Northern Irish artist, Cara Murphy featuring Her Majesty’s cypher.
In return, the Trumps gave the King and Queen a silver photo frame engraved with their joint cypher, a replica of a President Eisenhower sword and a Tiffany & Co. vintage 18K diamond and ruby flower brooch
The Trumps are currently having a lunch in the state dining room with members of the royal family, before viewing a special display of items relating to the US in the green drawing room.
Later, the president and first lady will visit St George’s Chapel to privately lay a wreath on the tomb of Queen Elizabeth.
The prime minister and Lady Starmer will then join them, alongside US and British military families, to view a Beating Retreat ceremony on the east lawn. The ceremony will conclude, if the weather allows, with a flypast by British and American F-35 military jets and the Red Arrows.
This evening, there’s a state banquet, which will include the prime minister and the leader of the opposition.
James Speed, 55, a school teacher, carried a flagpole with both the UK and Israeli flags outside the castle. He said he would have flown a US one had he owned one.
“I’ve come here to support the King because I was born here, but also to support the president of the United States coming here, because America and Britain are friends with a special relationship. I think anyone protesting Trump’s visit today needs to be very careful and respectful of what the United States has done for this country.”
He said he had received a few nasty comments about his Israeli flag but it had overall been respectful. “Our wonderful Jewish community in this country is feeling under threat,” he said. “The levels of antisemitism in this country are a disgrace.”
Protesters are gathering for a Stop Trump Coalition rally near the BBC at Portland Place. At least 80 groups — including the Palestine Solidarity Campaign, Stop the War coalition, Stand Up to Racism and climate groups — have signed up to demonstrate against the state visit of Trump, according to organisers.
People are holding an array of anti-Trump banners, signs, balloons of “baby Trump”, Palestinian and Ukrainian flags.
“We see Trump as the global spiritual leader of the far right, and we think Starmer is legitimising this violence by inviting Trump for a second state visit which is unnecessary”, said Seema Syeda, spokesperson for the stop trump coalition, and campaigner at Another Europe is Possible.
Syeda, 32, said that US president “is fuelling global war and genocide” in Gaza as well as fuelling the rise of fascism and violence and division on British streets. She added: “We need every person from every walk of life no matter what your identity is and your faith to join together and resist the rise of the far right and fascism because it will devour all of us.”
While many of those gathered close to the castle are taking a stand against President Trump’s policies, one group is protesting against the Chagos Island bill that will see the UK give the islands to Mauritius.
They waved flags and chanted: “What do we want, self-determination.”
Vanessa Mandarin Calou, 44, a campaigner from London, said: “My message for the US president is to speak to his Majesty, the king to save our British Island. You can’t get close to him [Trump] but our presence says everything, our flag says everything. They know that flag because it’s a beautiful flag and it represents our island. We have 16 British overseas islands and this one needs to be protected by the British people.”
Two local Liberal Democrat councillors stood holding signs, one of which read, “Windsor crown, not clown”, with a photo of Trump.
Another was a rainbow banner, which Mark Wilson said was in protest at Trump’s record on LGBTQ+ rights.
He added that residents felt angered by the road closures and fence along the Long Walk. He said they had “never seen such level of fortification”.
Amy Tisi agreed with the decision of the Liberal Democrat leader, Ed Davey, not to attend the state banquet this evening. “It’s absolutely right,” she said, “We are making a stand, we are using our democratic right to protest as he is.”
She added: “I would not like the King to be used as a pawn,” before saying: “We are very proud of the royal family in Windsor.”
Ed Davey, the Liberal Democrat leader, said he did not feel comfortable attending the state banquet for the US president, saying he wanted Trump to do more to end the war in Gaza.
“I felt that I wanted to go. I respect His Majesty and therefore I wanted to support him. But I really wrestled,” he told Times Radio.
“This is a genuinely difficult decision because I normally want to go to the state banquets to support His Majesty and indeed the British interests. But on deep reflection and consideration [I decided] that the best way to reflect the British interests was to take this stand.”
When asked why he was happy to attend the Qatari state visit but not Trump’s given Qatar’s funding of Hamas, Davey said Trump was in “unique position” to influence the Gaza conflict.
“I just hope government ministers will stand up and do the right thing and tell Trump to exercise his influence and stop it,” he said.
State visits are a crucial part of the “special relationship” between the UK and US, both a ceremonial set piece and a geopolitical chess move.
Yet official transatlantic visits by US heads of state are a relatively recent phenomenon and no two trips have been exactly alike. As the royal family prepare to welcome President Trump at Windsor this week, trade negotiations continue behind the scenes between No 10 and the White House.
Sir Keir Starmer has said that this “unprecedented” second state visit for a US president will feature “many elements” that have “never been seen before”. Trump has simply described his forthcoming visit as a “fest”.
• Read in full: State banquets, cups of tea and scones for ‘Uncle Ike’
Both the Queen and the Princess of Wales have showcased British fashion designers for the occasion.
Catherine was wearing a maroon-coloured Emilia Wickstead dress, hat by Jane Taylor and a feather brooch.
The Queen was wearing a sapphire blue dress, a coat by Fiona Clare and a hat by Philip Treacy.
President Trump saluted and his wife Melania held her hand to heart as the US anthem was played.
The president and King then began the formal inspection of the guard of honour. The overcast conditions have held off so far and there has not been any rain yet, although it has been quite windy.
The Massed Band played Jeremiah Clarke’s Trumpet Voluntary.
The Grenadier Guards can be distinguished by the white plume in their bearskin caps and singular buttons on their scarlet tunics.
The Coldstream Guards have red plumes in their bearskin caps and buttons in pairs on their tunics.
The Scots Guards’ bearskins have no plumes, the soldiers have thistles embroidered on their collars, and wear buttons in rows of three.
Inside the Quadrangle of Windsor Castle, a large guard of honour has been formed by detachments from the Nijmegen Company Grenadier Guards, the No 7 Company Coldstream Guards, and the F Company Scots Guards.
The units carry the state colours of each regiment, which are exceptionally large and heavy ceremonial silk flags, richly embroidered with symbols of historical relevance to the regiment.
Each weighs at least 10kg with the weight pitched at the carved heraldic end of the pole, making them extremely challenging to flourish. The state colours are carried by the most impressive young officer in the battalion.
The carriage’s route is lined by 22 half-companies of personnel.
The first section, from Rose Garden to Frogmore House, is lined by the Royal Navy Ceremonial Guard and the HM Royal Marines Band Portsmouth.
The second section, near the castle, is lined by the King’s Colour Squadron.
The third section, on Cambridge Drive, is lined by the 1st Battalion Irish Guards, 1st Battalion Grenadier Guards, 1st Battalion London Guards, Household Division and the Central Band of the Royal Air Force.
President Trump will join the King in the Irish State Coach for a ten-minute carriage procession through the grounds at Windsor towards the castle, while the Queen will be accompanied by the first lady in the Scottish State Coach. The Prince and Princess of Wales will follow in the Semi-State Landau.
The Honourable Warren Stephens, ambassador of the United States of America, and his wife; Marco Rubio, the US secretary of state and acting national security adviser, Scott Bessent, treasury secretary, Susie Wiles, assistant to the president and chief of staff, and Steve Witkoff, assistant to the president and special envoy for peace, will also take part.
The US and British National Anthems are played as the carriage procession moves off.
The procession will travel along Frogmore Drive and the George IV Gateway before arriving in the Quadrangle of Windsor Castle. The route is lined by Armed Forces personnel.
The president and first lady now join the King, Queen, William and Kate for a carriage procession through the grounds of Windsor, through George IV gate towards the Quandragle in the castle.
Exactly 80 soldiers ride as part of the sovereign’s escort, which accompanies the royal carriages.
It comprises four divisions and two standards (regimental flags) of the Life Guards and the Blues and Royals of the Household Cavalry Mounted Regiment, as well as farriers and serrefille captains.
The Life Guards wear red tunics and helmets with white plumes, while The Blues and Royals wear blue tunics and helmets with red plumes. The farriers are distinguished by the axes they carry on parade.
Trump saluted as he walked from Marine One with his wife Melania, to be greeted by the Prince and Princess of Wales.
The US president then walked hand-in-hand with his wife as they walked towards Windsor Castle.
They were then formally welcomed by the King and Queen outside Victoria House.
Trump and the first lady arrive accompanied by music from the Band of the Household Cavalry wearing state dress — a uniform designed in the 17th century and made from pure gold thread.
The Prince and Princess of Wales are the first to greet them in the grounds of Windsor Castle, before accompanying them to the King and Queen.
As the president shakes hands with the king, there will be a gun salutes of 41 rounds from six First World War-era guns on the East Lawn of Windsor Castle by The King’s Troop Royal Horse Artillery.
This will be joined by a simultaneous salute from the Tower of London by the Honourable Artillery Company, which is the City of London’s Army Reserve and regularly serves alongside US forces globally.
The US president has arrived at Windsor Castle.
Trump’s helicopter, Marine One, landed in the castle grounds just before 12.15pm, along with three other helicopters.
President Trump’s helicopter is only a few minutes from arriving at Windsor Castle.
Charles and Camilla, who was dressed in blue, have arrived at at Victoria House in preparation for the welcoming party for the US president on his second state visit to the UK.
The Queen is wearing a Sapphire blue dress, a coat by Fiona Clare and a hat by Philip Treacy, along with a sapphire and diamond brooch.
The Prince and Princess of Wales will lead the royal welcome for the president and first lady when they arrive by helicopter at the Walled Garden at Windsor Castle.
A Royal Salute will be fired by The King’s Troop Royal Horse Artillery from within the Home Park and another, simultaneously, at the Tower of London by The Honourable Artillery Company.
The Prince and Princess of Wales will then walk with the president and the first lady over to Victoria House, a former gardener’s cottage within the castle grounds, to meet The King and Queen.
Two students local to Windsor said they felt uncomfortable seeing Trump fans outside the castle and at their college.
Simran, 17, said, “I understand why he’s here, you can’t stop politics. But they’re doing so much for Trump and we don’t see the point. There’s so much excitement around it.”
On the projection of Trump and Epstein on to the castle yesterday, she said, “I’m glad that people are trying to make statements. Our voices need to be heard.”
She said she had seen an Israel flag which had “brought up inhumane political acts” and “tainted” the historic castle.

12.20pm: The president, accompanied by the King, will then inspect the Guard of Honour at Windsor Castle. After a visit to a special display of the Royal Collection items relating to the United States, the Trumps will then visit the late Queen Elizabeth II’s tomb in St George’s Chapel and lay a wreath
4.20pm: A group of 200 military musicians will perform a Beating Retreat on the East Lawn of Windsor Castle
4.35pm: A flypast by UK and US F-35 jets and the Red Arrows will take place
Evening: The traditional grand state banquet will take place at Windsor Castle tonight, where both Trump and the King are expected to give speeches
The Queen is well enough to attend all aspects of the state visit today, Buckingham Palace confirms
Lieutenant Colonel Storm Green, a South African officer of the Coldstream Guards in the British Army, will give the guard of honour’s commands before inviting President Trump to inspect the troops.
He said: “There are some nerves but that sort of apprehension makes you feel alive and like it’s an important event, which it is. It’s certainly the biggest state visit that I’ve taken part in, so there’s been a bit more rehearsal than normal.”
Green said all the practice was about ensuring it went smoothly on the day. He said: “Big events like this … you obviously want to do it well and show yourself off, show your organisation off and show your country off in the best possible light, so I’m keen to get it right.”
By Max Hastings
The roll call of groups supporting Wednesday’s “Trump Not Welcome” demonstration in London is predictable and cringe-making, headed by Extinction Rebellion, CND, Greenpeace and Southall Black Sisters. It is the sort of gathering mocked as Rent-A-Mob.
Yet my wife and I plan to turn out with them because it seems right to stand up and get counted among the naysayers when the most deplorable of all US presidents arrives on his second state visit to Britain.

Sir Keir Starmer hopes that President Trump’s visit can help to salvage what he describes as “phase two” of his premiership after a disastrous start.
But as ever with Trump, there are both big opportunities and significant risks. The Times assesses the potential wins for Starmer and where things could go badly wrong.

The lampposts in Windsor are lined with Union Jacks and US flags as police patrol in pairs.
Tourists and locals pass the castle slowly, surveying the road closure and security presence.
There are a few Maga hats in the crowd, as well as Union Jack-themed fancy dress for the occasion.
Rolph and Cheryl Schregardus from Wisconsin were in Windsor on the first leg of their visit the UK with their adult children.
They had not known about the state visit until they found themselves unable to book tickets to the castle.
Cheryl said they had voted for Trump in 2016 but had since changed their mind on him, as he had gone “overboard in what he’s doing”. Rolph said: “He’s a bully, he’s narcissistic, everything is for himself.”
On the ceremonial welcome Trump is due to receive today, he admitted it was important but said the US president “didn’t deserve it”.
In Windsor, Kaya Mar, an artist from London who paints political satire, was holding a picture of President Trump and the King outside the castle.
The painting, which had taken him two days, showed Trump as a stone age man wielding a spear and holding a baby-sized Charles in his grip.
Mar said: “He’s a bloody narcissistic Stone Age person. He thinks he’s a giant. If you come out here and shout that he’s a narcissist, the police will take you to the court so I say it with paint.”
Diane Clarke, 52, a teaching assistant from London, stood near the castle with a Maga flag and a T-shirt showing the moment Trump was shot and the words “Fight! Fight!”.
She had travelled to welcome Trump, who she described as a “peacemaker” and someone who “fought for freedom of speech”. Clarke said she felt moved that Trump would visit the Queen’s tomb later, adding: “I think that will really mean something to Trump and the first lady, really mean something.”
Clarke said the ceremony today was the “right amount” of welcome, although she was disappointed there would be no opportunity for the public to see him. She said: “We don’t all hate him, in fact it’s just the minority, the looney tunes left.” Although she admitted she had not yet met any Trump supporters in Windsor.
She said she felt “ashamed” of the protests against Trump, including the photo of him and Jeffrey Epstein that were projected onto the castle yesterday.
This is Trump’s second state visit to the UK — the first time the honour has been bestowed on a US president.
On his first state visit in June 2019, Trump and his wife Melania were greeted by Queen Elizabeth II and Prince Charles at Buckingham Palace.
The Trumps — who stayed at Winfield House, the US ambassador’s residence in Regent’s Park — were welcomed with a 41-gun salute at Green Park and Tower of London. That evening the couple attended a state banquet at Buckingham Palace hosted by the Queen.
On the second day of his trip, President Trump attended a business breakfast with the prime minister Theresa May, before bilateral talks at Downing Street.
On June 5, the final day of the state visit, the president and first lady joined commemorations for the 75th anniversary of D-Day in Portsmouth alongside other heads of state and government.
More than 6,300 police officers were deployed at a cost to the Metropolitan police of £3.4 million.
The president and first lady will travel to Windsor Castle, where they will be greeted by the Prince and Princess of Wales. They will be formally welcomed by the King and Queen with a royal salute fired from both the east lawn of the castle and the Tower of London.
All six will travel through the Windsor estate in a carriage procession, escorted by the Household Cavalry Mounted Regiment.
The Trumps will have lunch in the state dining room with members of the royal family and in the afternoon they will visit St George’s Chapel, to privately lay a wreath on Queen Elizabeth’s tomb.
The prime minister and Lady Starmer will then join them, alongside US and British military families, to view a Beating Retreat ceremony on the east lawn.
The ceremony will conclude, if the weather allows, with a flypast by British and American F-35 military jets and the Red Arrows.
By David Charter
Unlike most members of President Trump’s travelling party, for Scott Bessent the state visit is not a once-in-a-lifetime chance to rub shoulders with the royals. Instead it is merely the latest chapter in a long and remarkable friendship.
The 63-year-old US Treasury secretary’s close ties with the King and Queen go back three decades and include a role in aiding their public emergence as a couple after he established himself as a trusted confidant.
Bessent first met Charles in 1990 at the Charleston mansion of a close relative during a royal visit to South Carolina. He became a regular and generous donor to the Prince of Wales Foundation, Charles’s charity to support projects in education, healthcare, arts and the built environment.

President Trump had a verbal clash with an Australian journalist on the lawns of the White House just before he flew to the UK.
Trump was asked by John Lyons, a senior reporter with the Australian Broadcasting Corporation, about whether it was appropriate that a sitting president be engaged in business activity. “I’m really not, my kids are running the business,” a visibly annoyed Trump said.
The president then turned on the reporter. He said: “In my opinion, you are hurting Australia very much right now, and they want to get along with me.” Trump said he was going to be meeting with Anthony Albanese, the Australian prime minister, “very soon”, and added: “I’m going to tell him about you. You set a very bad tone.”
When Lyons tried to ask another question, Trump held his index finger to his lips and said “quiet” before asking for a question from another journalist.
A cabinet minister has distanced herself from her previous criticism of President Trump, saying that the US president is “fighting” for his country.
Liz Kendall, the science and technology secretary, declined to repeat her past comments about Trump in an interview this morning.
Speaking to BBC Radio 4’s Today programme, she said: “Actually, I’m more concerned about people like Elon Musk, with the violent rhetoric that he had over the weekend. What I believe about Donald Trump is that he is fighting for the United States, just as Keir is delivering for working people in this country.”
In 2016, Kendall tweeted: “Like most bullies, Trump doesn’t like it up him.” She has also previously accused Trump of undermining Nato, degrading the office of president and being a “populist” who ignored warnings about Russian interference in the 2016 US election.
Today’s military ceremonial welcome will be the largest for a state visit in living memory.
In total, about 120 horses and 1,300 members of the British military will welcome the president to Windsor Castle.
It is the first time there will be a joint UK-US military flypast at a state visit, with both UK and US F-35 fighter jets as well as the Red Arrows.
Windsor will also see the largest guard of honour and first Beating Retreat — a historic military pageant — at a state visit to the UK.
On Friday, a US military band will take part in Changing the Guard at Buckingham Palace for the first time in history.
Britain’s digital services tax will remain in place despite a deal with US tech companies, Kendall said. The science and technology secretary confirmed that the levy — charged at 2 per cent on the revenues of search engines and social media giants — would remain in place.
US firms have been lobbying to be exempt from it or have the tax lowered. But Kendall confirmed to Times Radio on Wednesday: “This is not included in the partnership … Rachel Reeves has been pretty straight with people saying we want people to pay their fair share of tax.”
The UK has also not made guarantees to the US about making it easier for their AI tools to access creative content made in Britain, said Kendall.
Music stars have warned against moves to let major US tech firms “harvest” their material without infringing copyright laws. But when asked if any guarantees had been made as part of the tech deal, Kendall said: “No we have not.”
The prime minister is hoping that significant deals will provide better news for the government.
Britain has signed a “tech prosperity deal” with the US that the government hopes will speed up the development of new medicines and improve collaboration on research in areas such as space exploration and defence.
Companies including Google, Microsoft, OpenAI and the chipmaker Nvidia are promising to build a wave of advanced computing power that ministers said would create thousands of jobs around the country.
Jensen Huang, founder of chip company Nvidia, which has agreed to deploy 120,000 advanced processors across the UK to help the British AI sector, praised the deal and said: “Today marks a historic chapter in US-United Kingdom technology collaboration. We are at the Big Bang of the AI era — and the United Kingdom stands in a Goldilocks position, where world-class talent, research and industry converge.”
The visit carries significant opportunities and risks. President Trump and Sir Keir Starmer differ publicly over Israel and the US has been heavily critical the UK’s decision to formally recognise Palestine as a state. Other potential areas of contention include free speech and Ukraine.
Ministers have been left disappointed by the failure to get a better deal on steel. In May, the prime minister struck a trade deal with Trump which included a pledge to eliminate tariffs on a proportion of UK steel and aluminium exports. At the time the deal was signed Starmer said it would “remove tariffs on British steel and aluminium, reducing them to zero”.
However, the UK has instead accepted a “permanent” 25 per cent tariff on exports after the US took a hardline stance in negotiations in recent days.
Protests against the state visit are “perhaps inevitable”, but it would not distract Sir Keir Starmer and the president from the historic trip, a cabinet minister said.
Liz Kendall, the technology secretary, told LBC: “They both want to deliver for their countries and their people.”
As protests are planned in London, hundreds of students have also pledged to walk out of schools, colleges and universities across the country on Wednesday.
Socialist Students, which is organising the protest, said: “The walkouts are a chance for young people to protest against Trump as well as Starmer’s Labour government, which has rolled out the red carpet for the US president.”
Police are preparing for a significant operation with as many as 50 protest groups expected to take to the streets of London to march against President Trump’s state visit.
More than 1,600 officers will be deployed on Wednesday — including 500 officers assisting from other forces, the Metropolitan police said.
Although the US president will not visit parliament, where the House of Commons will be in recess for party conference session, campaigners said they will demonstrate against what they called “our government’s choice to honour a man who is violating human rights in the United States and around the world”.
Stop Trump Coalition demonstrators will gather in Portland Place in central London on Wednesday afternoon before marching towards Parliament Square.
The rally will be compered by comedian Nish Kumar and writer Coco Khan, with speakers including the new leader of the Green Party Zack Polanski, the former Labour leader Jeremy Corbyn and Ben Jamal, the director of the Palestine Solidarity Campaign.
London residents were woken by the sound of military helicopters just before 10pm last night as the Trump entourage arrived at the US ambassador’s at Regent’s Park.
Earlier, police had closed off the outer circle of the park as they prepared for the arrival of the president and his entourage at Winfield House for an overnight stay.
Dozens of police officers fenced off the northern end of Regent’s Park in preparation for the presidential visit. The Grade II listed Winfield House is situated on 12 acres of land and has the second largest private garden in London after Buckingham Palace.
Trump said that the ambassador Warren Stephens was “doing really well” and said the “relationships are great”.
Asked about his feelings towards the UK, he said: “I love it. I love Turnberry, I love Aberdeen. I have a lot of things here that warm my heart. I want to tell you. It’s a very special place.”
Four people have been arrested on suspicion of malicious communications after images of President Trump and the paedophile financier Jeffrey Epstein were projected onto Windsor Castle, Thames Valley police said.
Chief Superintendent Felicity Parker said: “We take any unauthorised activity around Windsor Castle extremely seriously. Our officers responded swiftly to stop the projection and four people have been arrested.”
Political campaign group Led By Donkeys shared an image of the stunt to Instagram with the caption: “Hey Donald, welcome to Windsor Castle.” The four people remain in custody.
Speaking before his visit, Trump said that he wanted to “help” the UK on trade.
He said: “They want to see if they can refine the trade deal a little bit. We have made a deal, and it’s a great deal. And I’m into helping them. We’re having trillions come in because of the tariffs. They would like to see if they can get a little bit better deal.”
The president said that his trip was “primarily” about the King and Queen. He added: “They’re friends of mine for a long time, long before he was King. I think he represents the country so well. He’s such an elegant gentleman and he represents the country so well.”
President Trump and his wife, Melania, arrived in the UK on Tuesday evening for his historic second state visit.
The president and first lady were greeted by Yvette Cooper, the foreign secretary, at Stansted airport at the start of a three-day trip.
Today, Trump will be hosted by the King at Windsor Castle, where the pageantry will include a flypast by UK and US F-35 jets along with the Red Arrows. The day will culminate in a state dinner.
On Thursday, Trump will head to Chequers, the prime minister’s grace and favour home, where he and Starmer will hold a joint press conference.

On Monday about as many people knew the name of the Green Party’s then deputy leader as they did those of its actual leaders (Adrian Ramsay and Carla Denyer, to save you checking).
Even on the Tuesday lunchtime of Zack Polanski’s landslide victory in the party’s leadership contest, the BBC’s political editor Spoonerised his name. But after his appearances on everything from Newsnight to, on only three hours’ sleep, Good Morning Britain, millions now know who Polanski is.
With his fluency, courtesy and trick of listening carefully to questions that he then answers directly, the Greens’ new leader is suddenly Britain’s most charismatic politician — if we forget, for a moment, Nigel Farage. And that, I realise as I interview him on a thunderous afternoon in a café over the bridge from parliament, could make him very dangerous indeed.
To some in his own party — perhaps the 15 per cent who voted for his rivals — his was a “hostile takeover” of a venerable ecological movement by a leftist who was not even an MP. Jewish, he changed his surname at 18 to that of his family’s East European ancestors, a defiant gesture against antisemites.
Yet he accuses Israel of genocide in Gaza. He calls for Thames Water to be taken into public ownership, and for higher taxes on inheritance, capital gains and mega-wealth. After the Supreme Court defined women biologically in April, he Instagrammed that “trans rights are human rights”.
But Polanski’s threat is not only to genteel ecologists. If in 2029 he strikes — as he has not ruled out — an electoral pact with Jeremy Corbyn and Zarah Sultana’s new party, this 42-year-old chairman of the London Assembly fire committee could help Farage blow up Britain’s 2.5-party system itself.
“I mean, let’s be honest, Kemi Badenoch is barely worth even discussing. I think it’s very clear that she’s not cut through with the country and she’s absolutely failed,” he begins when I ask him what I think of the prime minister and leader of the opposition. “And from Keir Starmer, I think we have a deeply cynical, disappointing sell-out as a prime minister.”
He believes Labour is scared of him, which is why after his election it tweeted a passage from a 2013 edition of The Sun reporting that, during an unlikely spell as a Harley Street hypnotherapist, he told a reporter he could enlarge her breasts with his mind. (He replied that he apologised for his mistake and at least had “never armed a genocide”.) In his view, Labour would have been smarter to welcome his election. But, I say, he started the war in his acceptance speech by saying he wanted the Greens to replace Labour. “And I absolutely do.”
“Keir Starmer is absolutely terrified of the Green Party right now and so he should be. I think Keir Starmer is doing everything he can to alienate people at every moment, from the two-child benefit cap, the disability cap, his refusal to attack the super-rich, and of course the ongoing genocide in Gaza.”
But the government doesn’t want to be unpopular, I protest. It is unpopular because there’s no money. It is paying £100 billion a year in debt interest and the bond market’s about to go crazy.
“I really disagree. Since the pandemic began, billionaire wealth in this country has doubled while our public assets have been stripped away. I think what we’ve seen over and over again is a movement of public money towards private wealth and it shouldn’t surprise us that the Labour government is doing this. This is a party that took £4.1 million from venture capital during the general election. These are hedge funds with assets in oil and gas, gambling companies and arms trades.”
So they’re in hock to big business and finance? “Oh, entirely, vested interests. I would rather they wore it on their shirts so we knew who is sponsoring them. The Green Party has two vested interests. It’s the people and the planet.”
I am enjoying this, but remind myself he has form for entrancing people. He sounds plausible, I say, but these are the politics I usually hear from raggedy blokes shouting “smash the rich” outside Sainsbury’s on Saturday mornings. “Well, there’s a lot of wisdom in our communities and I think some of what we’re talking about here is the tone that you use and the way that you communicate things.”
• Whose side are you on? Green Zack Polanski will tell you
Yet I am worried. All my life elections have been won on the centre ground by parties that are themselves coalitions. Now we may be heading for an election between an extreme-right party led by Farage and an extreme-left coalition of Greens and Corbyn-Sultanas.
“Yeah, I really reject the phrase extreme left.” But he’s to the left of Corbyn, isn’t he? “I think it depends if you’re talking about economics or social issues”
It still frightens me politics has become so polarised. “I’m definitely very, very concerned about the far right and the rise of the far right. I’m also concerned about what used to be called centrism, where the Labour Party and the Tory party are, because I think they’ve swung to the right too. I think the centre has massively shifted.”
• New Greens leader eyes more votes with left-wing populism
He calls his politics eco-populist but isn’t the great populist cause of the day the movement against asylum seekers? Have its supporters all been groomed by Farage? Do they labour under false-consciousness? Perhaps it is actually how they feel.
“I think it is how people feel and I genuinely think they’re feeling those feelings,” he replies. “This is the dangerous side of populism if you don’t win the argument with your values, if you just go to where you think a mob might be — for instance, outside an asylum hotel, as we’ve seen [Tory frontbencher] Robert Jenrick doing explicitly. Nigel Farage calls himself a patriot but I’m very clear that Nigel Farage hates communities that don’t look like the communities he wants them to look like.”
Does he have a Union Jack in his home? “No, and I think it’s weird to have a Union Jack in your place. I think that [idea] has been imported from America. If it’s during a football game I will paint the St George’s cross on my face, because that’s context appropriate.”
Green values are about co-operation, he says. So why not build bridges with green Tories such as John Gummer, Theresa May and William Hague? “Those are Conservatives who are very much no longer on the front line of politics. I think they’re pretty horrified of where the party’s been going.”
But how green is he actually? The Hackney urbanite says he has always loved nature and country walks, rides a bike, is carless and a vegan but that equality is the prerequisite to tackling climate change. It is just, I say to the former Liberal Democrat, people may wonder if his would-be viral politics have simply found a host in the Green Party. I mean, had I met him ten years ago would his politics have been green or left? “Ten years ago I wouldn’t have been talking about either of these things at all. I was totally uninterested in politics.”
And it is now he tells me the story of his life, and of the greening of Zack Polanski. He was born in Salford, not, he jokes, to a toolmaker but a purveyor of tools at a DIY store. His mother — his parents later divorced — worked as a TV make-up artist. He won a scholarship to the fee-paying Stockport Grammar School but hated it. At 14 or 15, he came out as gay.
“I was being homophobically bullied and I often felt that I was the problem as opposed to a person that needs to be helped. I then was asked to leave the school at sixth form because I’d been a little bit too cheeky.” At Ridge Danyers sixth-form college he was much happier and went on to study drama at Aberystwyth University. He became a stage actor, taught, and ended up in the community company Theatre of the Oppressed. Only then did politics tempt him, first the Lib Dems and then the Remain cause. He ran into Extinction Rebellion and, sceptical at first, realised it was time to be “bold and ambitious”. When he met the Green leader Natalie Bennett, he found his political home.
In 2018 he was among the Extinction Rebellion supporters arrested for blocking Westminster Bridge. He spent the night in a police cell but not charged. “It made me even more committed.”
I ask when he first trod the boards. It was at school, an attempt by his parents to “channel my cheekiness”. He was Puck in A Midsummer Night’s Dream, a part he would later play professionally. “What I love about Puck is he’s a happy warrior, and if I was going to characterise how I wanted to be as a Green Party leader, I think it’s a happy warrior.”
He recalls Puck’s address to the audience at the play’s end: “If we shadows have offended…” He says: “That’s a moment about authentic communication that still carries over with me now.”
But equally people might say actors are professional liars, adept at selling ice to Inuit and convincing women they can increase their cup size. “This is esoteric but it’s also very, very important and you could ask any professional good actor. Acting is not about lying. It’s not even about falsity. Acting is about authentic communication.”
Certainly, he was not faking it when during his victory address he choked up thanking his partner, Richie Bryan, a palliative care worker whom he met eight or so years ago, and whom he “loves deeply”. He says: “The public want to know that politicians are human. I think far too many of our politicians are absolutely robotic, dull and aren’t able to communicate. I think that’s why this country is in the state it’s in.”
And talking of authenticity, is he going to do something about his missing left tooth? “Absolutely not. My boyfriend loves my smile. I’m happy with my smile. I don’t think we need artifice in our politicians.” Until last year a baby tooth remained in place there. Its adult replacement may yet arrive. The coming wisdom, I say. “Nice,” he replies. “I’m going to patent that: the coming wisdom.”
From, perhaps, the coming man.
